mainTopic: How the wording of vows and oaths decides whether they take effect, and how נדרים differ from שבועות
overview: The גמרא asks whose view our משנה about קרבן vows follows. It answers רבי מאיר, because רבי יהודה does not make the wording distinctions the משנה relies on. A challenge comes from an earlier משנה where רבי מאיר forbids 'לקרבן, I will not eat of yours.' The גמרא answers that our משנה is about 'לא לקרבן', meaning 'not a קרבן', which makes no vow. Next, a new משנה rules that several oath wordings forbid the food, including 'שבועה שאוכל לך.' A משנה in מסכת שבועות seems to read 'שאוכל' as 'I will eat.' אביי answers that the meaning depends on whether he was agreeing to eat or refusing. רב אשי instead reads the word as 'שאי אוכל', and the גמרא explains why each one rejected the other's answer. Finally, a new משנה teaches that oaths are stricter than vows in one way, and vows are stricter in another: a נדר can forbid using a סוכה, לולב or תפילין, but a שבועה to break a מצוה does not take effect.

steps.title: Whose view is the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking which תנא wrote our משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: Whose opinion does the משנה follow?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by asking which תנא our משנה follows. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה makes careful distinctions about the exact wording of a vow. Not every תנא agrees that such small wording changes matter. So the גמרא wants to know whose opinion the משנה reflects.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion on the משנה
Who? Whose opinion?
Our משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA: Whose opinion is the משנה?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the discussion on the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא is the author of the משנה's rulings on vows that use the word קרבן.

steps.title: It follows רבי מאיר, not רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה must be רבי מאיר, because רבי יהודה treats 'קרבן' and 'הקרבן' the same way.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is רבי מאיר. If it were רבי יהודה, that would not work, because for him it makes no difference whether one said 'an offering' or 'the offering.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה follows רבי מאיר. It proves this by showing that רבי יהודה's view does not fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה treats different wordings differently. Some forms with 'קרבן' or 'הקרבן' do not take effect, while other forms do. רבי יהודה holds that a vow only works if one says 'like an offering' (כְּקָרְבָּן). So for him, plain 'קרבן' and 'הקרבן' are the same, and neither works. That leaves רבי מאיר as the author.

keyTerms.meaning: An offering; a word used to make food forbidden through a vow
The offering
It makes no difference to him
Because if

phrases.english: It is רבי מאיר.
For if it were רבי יהודה,
it makes no difference to him whether one says 'an offering'
and no difference whether one says 'the offering.'
phrases.notes: For רבי יהודה, neither wording makes a vow, since he needs 'like an offering.'

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר הִיא, דְּאִי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה follows רבי מאיר, because רבי יהודה does not make the wording distinctions the משנה relies on.

steps.title: Quoting the end of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the last clause of the משנה: 'לקרבן, I will not eat of yours' is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now look at the last part of the משנה: if someone says 'For an offering, I will not eat of yours,' the food is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the end of the משנה to test the answer it just gave. This is a setup for a challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules that this wording does not make a vow, so the food stays permitted. If the משנה is רבי מאיר, then רבי מאיר should agree with this ruling. The next step checks whether he really does.

keyTerms.meaning: Say the last clause; look at the end of the משנה
Permitted
For an offering

phrases.english: Say the last clause of the משנה:
'For an offering, I will not eat of yours' — it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the answer of step 2 against the end of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the end of the משנה, saying 'For an offering, I will not eat of yours' leaves the food permitted.

steps.title: But רבי מאיר forbids this wording
steps.stepSummary: An earlier משנה says רבי מאיר forbids the food in this exact case, and רבי אבא explains why. So the end of our משנה cannot be רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in a משנה: 'For an offering, I will not eat of yours' — רבי מאיר forbids. And רבי אבא said: it is as if he said, 'Let it be for an offering, and therefore I will not eat of yours.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges its own answer. An earlier משנה shows that רבי מאיר forbids the food in the very case our משנה permits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבא explains that רבי מאיר reads the words as two parts. First, 'let your food be like an offering to me.' Then, 'therefore I will not eat it.' That makes a real vow. So רבי מאיר would forbid what our משנה permits, and the answer 'it is רבי מאיר' now seems to fail as well.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't we learn in a משנה?
Forbids
It is treated as if he said
Therefore

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two מִשְׁנָיוֹת. Our משנה says this wording is permitted. The earlier משנה says רבי מאיר forbids it. That clash is the whole problem.
steps.whyThisMatters: With both רבי יהודה and רבי מאיר seemingly ruled out, the גמרא now needs a new way to explain who the משנה follows.

phrases.english: But didn't we learn: 'For an offering, I will not eat of yours' —
phrases.notes: This is the earlier משנה on 13a.

phrases.english: רבי מאיר forbids.
And רבי אבא said:
It is treated as if he said: 'Let it be for an offering,'
'therefore I will not eat of yours.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתְנַן: ״לַקׇּרְבָּן לֹא אוֹכַל לָךְ״ — רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹסֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the clause quoted in step 3 to attack the answer of step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 2 that our משנה follows רבי מאיר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Our משנה permits 'For an offering, I will not eat of yours.' But an earlier משנה says רבי מאיר forbids it, and רבי אבא explains that he reads it as a real vow. So the משנה cannot be רבי מאיר.

steps.title: Two different sentences: 'as a קרבן' versus 'not a קרבן'
steps.stepSummary: The two משניות are talking about different wordings. 'לַקׇּרְבָּן' makes a vow, but 'לָא לְקׇרְבָּן' means 'it should not be a קרבן', so no vow takes effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. That משנה is about someone who said 'לַקׇּרְבָּן' (as a קרבן). This משנה is about someone who said 'לָא לְקׇרְבָּן' (no, not a קרבן). He is saying that it should not be a קרבן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction from step 4. The two משניות are talking about two different sentences, so רבי מאיר can still be the author of our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier משנה the person said 'לַקׇּרְבָּן', meaning 'as a קרבן, I will not eat yours', and רבי מאיר says that vow works. In our משנה the person said 'לָא לְקׇרְבָּן', and the word 'לָא' turns it into 'it should NOT be a קרבן'. That is the opposite of a vow, so the food stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. This is how the גמרא opens an answer that shows two sources do not really clash.
'As a קרבן.' This works as a real vow.
'No, not a קרבן.' It takes away the vow instead of making one.

steps.whatToRemember: One small word, 'לָא', changes everything. With it, the person is saying 'not a קרבן', so no vow takes effect, and our משנה can still be רבי מאיר.
steps.confusionAlert: The two phrases look almost the same, but they mean opposite things. 'לַקׇּרְבָּן' makes a vow. 'לָא לְקׇרְבָּן' means 'not a קרבן', so there is no vow.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
That [earlier משנה] is where he said 'For a קרבן,'
this [our משנה] is where he said 'Not for a קרבן' —
he is saying that it should not be a קרבן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: the two משניות are talking about different wordings.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought both משניות were about the same phrase 'לקרבן', so רבי מאיר would contradict himself.
steps.terutzMaskana: Our משנה is about 'לָא לְקׇרְבָּן' ('not a קרבן'), which is no vow. So רבי מאיר can be its author.

steps.title: New משנה: oaths about not eating someone's food
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists three ways of phrasing a שבועה about someone's food. In all of them the food is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If one says 'An oath, I will not eat of yours', or 'This is an oath that I will eat of yours', or 'No! An oath, I will not eat of yours', the food is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It moves from vows that use the word 'קרבן' to oaths that use the word 'שבועה'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three wordings forbid the food, even the ones that look odd, like 'that I will eat' or the phrase that opens with 'לָא'. With a קרבן, 'לָא' cancelled the vow. Here, with a שבועה, the משנה says the person is still bound. The גמרא that follows explains only the 'that I will eat' wording.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה. It marks the start of a new משנה.
An oath. It binds the person himself, while a vow (נדר) forbids the object.
Forbidden.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not be thrown by 'that I will eat' leading to 'forbidden'. The גמרא is about to explain how this wording really means a promise not to eat.

phrases.english: MISHNA: 'An oath, I will not eat of yours,'
'This is an oath that I will eat of yours,'

phrases.aramaic: לָא שְׁבוּעָה לֹא אוֹכַל לָךְ — אָסוּר.
phrases.english: 'No! An oath, I will not eat of yours' — it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. The topic moves from 'קרבן' vows to oaths.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath not to eat someone's food, in any of these three wordings, makes the food forbidden to the one who swore.

steps.title: Inference from the משנה: 'שאוכל לך' means 'I will not eat'
steps.stepSummary: Our משנה forbids the food when someone says 'שבועה שאוכל לך,' so this wording must mean 'I swear I will not eat of yours.'
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: We learn from this that 'an oath that I will eat of yours' means 'that I will not eat.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a lesson from the wording of our משנה. This sets up the next move, where a different משנה will seem to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה said that 'שבועה שאוכל לך' makes the friend's food forbidden. That only works if the words mean 'I swear I will not eat yours.' So the plain-sounding 'that I will eat' is really being read as a refusal.

keyTerms.meaning: By inference; we can learn from this
An oath 'that I will eat of yours'
It means; it implies
I eat / I will eat (Aramaic)

steps.confusionAlert: Read literally, 'שבועה שאוכל' sounds like 'I swear I WILL eat.' The משנה reads it as 'I swear I will NOT eat.' That gap is the whole puzzle of this section.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
By inference, this teaches that
'An oath that I will eat of yours'
means 'that I will not eat.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a meaning from the oath wordings listed in the משנה in Step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'שבועה שאוכל לך' means 'I swear I will not eat of yours.'

steps.title: Contradiction from the משנה in מסכת שבועות
steps.stepSummary: A משנה in מסכת שבועות lists 'שאוכל' next to 'שלא אוכל' as opposites. That shows 'שאוכל' means 'I will eat.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And they raised a contradiction: There are two kinds of oaths that are really four: 'that I will eat' and 'that I will not eat,' 'that I ate' and 'that I did not eat.' That משנה separately says 'that I will not eat' and 'that I did not eat.' So 'that I will eat of yours' must mean 'that I will eat'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different משנה that seems to clash with what we just learned. There, 'שאוכל' means 'I will eat.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה in שבועות puts 'שאוכל' and 'שלא אוכל' side by side. If 'שאוכל' already meant 'I will not eat,' there would be no reason to list 'שלא אוכל' separately. So that משנה treats 'שאוכל' as a positive oath, which goes against our inference.

keyTerms.meaning: And they pointed out a contradiction
Two kinds of oaths that are really four
That I will not eat
That I ate (an oath about the past)

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
Oaths are two, which are really four.
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in מסכת שבועות: two basic kinds (future and past), each with a 'yes' and a 'no' version.

phrases.english: 'That I will eat' and 'that I will not eat,'
'that I ate' and 'that I did not eat.'
Since it says 'that I will not eat'
and 'that I ate' and 'that I did not eat' as separate items,
we learn that 'that I will eat of yours'
means 'that I will eat'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inference of Step 7 with a contradicting משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that 'שבועה שאוכל לך' means 'I will not eat.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה in שבועות lists 'שאוכל' and 'שלא אוכל' as opposites, so 'שאוכל' must mean 'I will eat.'

steps.title: אביי: 'שאוכל' can mean either one, depending on context
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that 'שאוכל' can be read two ways. If he had been saying 'I will eat,' it means he will eat. If he had been refusing, it means he will not eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: 'שאוכל' can mean two things. If people were pressing him to eat, and he said 'I will eat, I will eat,' and then added 'an oath that I will eat,' it means 'I will eat.' But if he said 'I will not eat, I will not eat,' and then added 'an oath that I will eat,' he means 'I will not eat.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי settles the contradiction. The same word means different things depending on what the person was saying just before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words alone do not decide. The setting does. After 'I will eat,' the oath backs up that promise to eat, which is the case in מסכת שבועות. After 'I will not eat,' the oath backs up the refusal, which is the case in our משנה. So both משניות are right, each in its own setting.

keyTerms.meaning: It can mean two different things
They were pressing him; urging him
And then also; furthermore
He is saying; this is what he means

steps.whatToRemember: 'שבועה שאוכל' gets its meaning from the conversation around it. After 'I will eat,' it is an oath to eat. After 'I will not eat,' it is an oath not to eat.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a key idea in the laws of vows and oaths: we read a person's words in light of the setting he spoke them in, not just their literal grammar.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
'That I will eat' can mean two different things.
If they were pressing him to eat,
and he said: 'I will eat, I will eat,'
and then added: 'An oath that I will eat,'
it means 'that I will eat.'
phrases.notes: This fits the משנה in מסכת שבועות.

phrases.english: But if he said: 'I will not eat, I will not eat,'
and then added: 'An oath that I will eat,'
he means 'that I will not eat.'
phrases.notes: This fits our משנה, where the food was forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: שֶׁאוֹכַל שְׁתֵּי לְשׁוֹנוֹת מַשְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing cases by context: the same word carries different meanings in different settings.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'שאוכל' has one fixed meaning, so the two משניות contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'שאוכל' means 'I will eat' after he said he would eat, and 'I will not eat' after he refused. Each משנה describes one of these settings.

steps.title: רב אשי: He really said 'that I will not eat'
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers the contradiction differently from אביי: the 'שאוכל' of our משנה is really 'שאי אוכל', meaning 'that I will not eat.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The 'שאוכל' in our משנה about a שבועה really means he said 'שאי אוכל', 'that I will not eat.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a second, different way to solve the contradiction between our משנה and the משנה in מסכת שבועות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי said the same word can mean opposite things depending on context. רב אשי says the word itself was really different: the person said 'שאי אוכל', which clearly means 'I will not eat.' So the משנה in מסכת שבועות, where 'שאוכל' means 'I will eat,' is not contradicted.

keyTerms.meaning: 'That I will not eat': a negative oath
He is saying (what he actually said)

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
The 'that I will eat' of the oath in our Mishnah —
he is saying 'that I will not eat.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer from אביי's to the same contradiction (Step 8).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the wording: the word was really 'שאי אוכל'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'שאוכל' in our משנה seemed to mean 'I will eat,' which contradicts the food becoming forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: The person actually said 'שאי אוכל', so it is a clear oath not to eat.

steps.title: If so, why teach something so obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב אשי: if he plainly said 'I will not eat,' of course the food is forbidden. Why would the משנה need to say it?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, it is obvious! Why does it need to be said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב אשי's answer by saying it makes the משנה teach something nobody would doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the person clearly swore 'I will not eat of yours,' there is no question that the food is forbidden to him. A משנה is not supposed to teach something so plain, so רב אשי's reading seems to make the משנה pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious
Why does it need to be said?

phrases.english: If so, it is obvious!
Why does it need to be said?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אשי's answer from Step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's reading that the person said 'שאי אוכל'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the wording is plainly negative, the ruling is obvious and the משנה would have no reason to teach it.

steps.title: We might have thought he slipped in his speech
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: we might have thought he tripped over his words and really meant 'I will eat,' so the משנה teaches that we go by what he said.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: he stumbled in getting his words out (and really meant 'I will eat'). So the משנה teaches us (that he meant 'I will not eat').
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב אשי by showing the משנה does teach something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because 'שאי אוכל' sounds so close to 'שאוכל', we might suspect he meant to say 'I will eat' and just slipped. The משנה teaches that we do not assume a slip: his words count as 'I will not eat,' and the food is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces a mistaken assumption)
Stumbled, tripped up
It teaches us (the new point)

phrases.english: You might have said:
he stumbled in getting the words out,
phrases.notes: Literally 'in setting up the words he tripped,' meaning maybe he really wanted to say 'I will eat.'

phrases.english: so it teaches us (that he meant 'I will not eat').

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: מֵיקַם לִישָּׁנָא הִיא דְּאִיתְּקִיל לֵיהּ, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 11 and saves רב אשי's reading.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing a real חידוש: ruling out the possibility of a speech slip
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe he slurred his words and actually meant 'I will eat.'
steps.terutzMaskana: We take his words as 'I will not eat,' and the food is forbidden.

steps.title: Why אביי did not answer like רב אשי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that אביי did not use רב אשי's answer because the משנה says 'שאוכל', not 'שאי אוכל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי did not give the reason of רב אשי, because the משנה does not say 'שאי אוכל' (it says 'שאוכל').
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why אביי needed his own answer instead of using רב אשי's simpler one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי's answer requires reading a word into the משנה that is not written there. אביי prefers to keep the משנה's actual wording, 'שאוכל', and explain that this very word can mean 'I will not eat' depending on context.

keyTerms.meaning: Reason, explanation
It teaches (what the משנה actually says)

steps.whatToRemember: Two answers to why 'שבועה שאוכל לך' forbids the food: אביי says the word 'שאוכל' can mean 'I will not eat' when he was refusing to eat. רב אשי says he really said 'שאי אוכל'. אביי rejects that because the משנה's wording is 'שאוכל'.

phrases.aramaic: אַבָּיֵי לָא אָמַר טַעַם כְּרַב אָשֵׁי —
phrases.english: Abaye did not give the reason of Rav Ashi —
because the Mishnah does not teach 'that I will not eat.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּיֵי לָא אָמַר טַעַם כְּרַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two answers (Steps 9 and 10) and explains why אביי did not adopt רב אשי's.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רב אשי's reading only from אביי's point of view
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה's actual wording is 'שאוכל', not 'שאי אוכל', so רב אשי's reading does not match the text.

steps.title: Why רב אשי turned away from אביי's reasoning
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי did not accept אביי's answer. If context can change what 'שאוכל' means, then 'שלא אוכל' could also mean two things. For example, someone being pressed to eat might say 'שבועה שלא אוכל' and really mean 'I will eat.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי turned away from אביי's reason. He held that 'that I will not eat' could also carry two meanings. Picture people pressing a man to eat, and he says, 'I'm not eating, I'm not eating,' and then adds 'שבועה.' Whether he then said 'that I will eat' or 'that I will not eat,' it means he is saying 'I will eat.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains why רב אשי did not accept אביי's answer. He shows that אביי's logic would also flip the meaning of 'שלא אוכל.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי let the situation decide what 'שאוכל' means. רב אשי points out that the same move works on 'שלא אוכל.' Said to the people pressing him, it can sound like 'An oath that I won't eat? Of course I'll eat!' So in that case, both phrases would end up meaning 'I will eat.'

keyTerms.meaning: turned away from, moved off (a reasoning)
reason, reasoning
two possible meanings
pressing him, urging him
I eat / I will eat (Aramaic)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא says קסבר ('he held'), so this is רב אשי's own reasoning, not a ruling that 'שלא אוכל' is really ambiguous. He is showing where אביי's logic would lead if we followed it all the way.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב אָשֵׁי נָאדֵי מִן טַעַם דְּאַבָּיֵי.
phrases.english: And Rav Ashi turned away from Abaye's reason,
because he held that 'that I will not eat' also
can mean two things.
If they were pressing him to eat,
and he said: 'I'm not eating, I'm not eating,'
and he also said: 'An oath,'
whether he said 'that I will eat' or 'that I will not eat,'
this means he is saying 'I will eat.'
phrases.notes: Read 'שלא אוכל' here like a question: 'Did I swear not to eat? No, I'll eat!'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב אָשֵׁי נָאדֵי מִן טַעַם דְּאַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 13 explained why אביי did not use רב אשי's answer. Now the גמרא explains the other side: why רב אשי did not use אביי's answer.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: אביי's answer that 'שאוכל' carries two meanings depending on the situation.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The same logic would make 'שלא אוכל' ambiguous too. That clashes with the clear rule taught by the תנא.

steps.title: The plain reading of 'I will not eat' is also possible
steps.stepSummary: 'שבועה שלא אוכל' can also be read simply, as 'an oath that I will not eat.' So under אביי's approach, the phrase would swing between two meanings.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the phrase 'an oath that I will not eat' can also be explained simply: he is saying 'an oath that I won't eat.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds that 'שלא אוכל' also keeps its plain meaning. This finishes showing that under אביי's logic the phrase becomes ambiguous. It also sets up the closing proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 showed that 'שלא אוכל' could mean 'I will eat.' This step shows it can also mean 'I won't eat.' So if we follow אביי, both oath phrases become unclear, and the next step shows why that cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: it is possible to explain it
the wording, the expression

phrases.english: And one can also explain the wording
'an oath that I will not eat'
as him saying 'an oath that I will not eat.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the point from step 14: 'שלא אוכל' would have two meanings, the reversed one and the plain one.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: אביי's approach of reading oath words based on the situation.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Under that approach, 'שלא אוכל' has both a reversed meaning and a plain meaning, so it is no longer clear.

steps.title: The תנא fixed one clear meaning for each phrase
steps.stepSummary: The תנא stated a clear rule: 'שאוכל' means 'I will eat,' and 'שלא אוכל' means 'I will not eat.' Since the meanings are fixed, אביי's two-meanings approach cannot stand. That is why רב אשי reads our משנה as 'שאי אוכל.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the תנא ruled clearly: 'that I will eat' means 'I will eat,' and 'that I will not eat' means 'I will not eat.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the proof that settles why רב אשי rejected אביי. The תנא gave each phrase one firm meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'אלא' (rather) cuts off the idea that the situation can change the meaning. The תנא treats both phrases as having one fixed meaning. A reading where 'שאוכל' can mean 'I won't eat' does not fit that, so רב אשי had to change the wording of the משנה to 'שאי אוכל' instead.

keyTerms.meaning: the teacher of the משנה
ruled it clearly, set it firmly
means, implies

steps.whatToRemember: אביי: 'שאוכל' can mean 'I will eat' or 'I won't eat,' depending on the situation. רב אשי: that cannot be, because the תנא fixed one meaning for each phrase. So our משנה must really read 'שאי אוכל.'
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the basic disagreement. אביי lets the situation shape what oath words mean. רב אשי holds that the תנא's wording rules are fixed, even if that means changing how we read the משנה.

phrases.english: Rather, the Tanna ruled it clearly:
phrases.notes: This is the תנא who teaches the oath rules in מסכת שבועות.

phrases.english: 'that I will eat' means 'I will eat,'
and 'that I will not eat' means 'I will not eat.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the תנא's clear rule to finish rejecting אביי's approach from steps 14 and 15.
steps.raayaObject: רב אשי's rejection of אביי, and his reading of the משנה as 'שאי אוכל.'
steps.raayaSupportSource: The תנא's fixed rule: 'שאוכל' means 'I will eat,' and 'שלא אוכל' means 'I will not eat.'

steps.title: Oaths are stricter than vows in one way
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה opens by saying that the rule just taught is an area where שבועות are stricter than נדרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is a way that oaths are stricter than vows.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It names a rule as a place where a שבועה is stronger than a נדר, and this sets up the opposite case in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'זה' ('this') refers to a rule about oaths and vows: a שבועה can take effect even on an action with no physical substance. A נדר works by forbidding a thing, so it does not take effect on such actions. This sets up the second half of the משנה, which shows the reverse.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה. It marks the start of a new משנה.
A stringency, a way in which something is stricter.
Oaths, where a person binds himself to do or not do something.
Vows, where a person forbids an item or a benefit to himself.

phrases.english: MISHNA: This is a stringency of oaths over vows,
phrases.notes: 'This' refers to the rule that an oath can take effect on an action with no physical substance, but a vow cannot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה begins after the גמרא's discussion of 'שאוכל' and 'שלא אוכל' ends. It names a stringency of שבועות over נדרים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שבועה can take effect on an action with no physical substance, and a נדר cannot. In this way שבועות are stricter than נדרים.

steps.title: Vows are stricter than oaths: a vow can forbid a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה gives the reverse case. A קונם against making a סוכה, taking a לולב, or putting on תפילין takes effect as a נדר, but not as a שבועה, because one cannot swear to break the מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And there is a way that vows are stricter than oaths. How so? Suppose someone said: 'Making a סוכה is קונם for me,' or 'Taking a לולב is קונם for me,' or 'Putting on תפילין is קונם for me.' As a vow, it is forbidden to him. As an oath, it is permitted, because a person cannot swear to break the מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה shows where a נדר is stronger than a שבועה. A נדר can stop a person from using a מצוה item, but a שבועה to skip a מצוה does not take effect at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נדר forbids the item itself to the person, so the סוכה, לולב or תפילין become forbidden to him, and the נדר stands. A שבועה binds the person to act or not act. The משנה says one cannot swear to break the מצוות, so such a שבועה is empty and he stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: How so? It introduces an example.
A word used to make a נדר. It declares something forbidden like a קרבן.
Forbidden.
Permitted.
To break the מצוות, to go against what the תורה commands.

steps.whatToRemember: A נדר can take effect even against a מצוה, because it forbids the item. A שבועה to break a מצוה does not take effect at all.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the נדר makes the מצוה stop being a מצוה. The מצוה stays the same. This person just cannot use these items while his נדר stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the basic difference between a נדר and a שבועה that runs through all of מסכת נדרים.

phrases.english: And there is a stringency of vows over oaths.
How so? If he said:
'A סוכה that I make is קונם (for me),'
phrases.notes: He means: making a סוכה is forbidden to me like a קרבן.

phrases.english: 'A לולב that I take,'
'תפילין that I put on' —
with vows, it is forbidden,
with oaths, it is permitted,
because one cannot swear to break the commandments.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It completes the משנה. Step 17 gave the stringency of שבועות, and this step gives the opposite stringency of נדרים, with an example.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A קונם against using a מצוה item (סוכה, לולב, תפילין) takes effect as a נדר. The same words as a שבועה do not take effect, because one cannot swear to break the מצוות.
